title: Snow Is a Glacier’s Shield—and Its Building Material
summary:
Snow is more than a white blanket on a glacier. It protects old ice and can help create new ice, too.

That matters in Switzerland, where scientists say glaciers lost 5.5 percent of their ice volume this year. It was the second-largest percentage loss on record. Heat waves and low winter snowfall contributed to the melt.

Matthias Huss, who leads the GLAMOS glacier monitoring service, explains snow's two jobs. Snow cover protects the ice underneath from melting. Snow that stays high in the mountains can also become new glacier ice.

Over five years, Swiss glaciers have lost nearly a fifth of their ice volume, experts report. Scientists are measuring the changes and even adding red dye to streams to follow where meltwater goes.

Why study these icy mountains? Switzerland supplies water to important European rivers, including the Rhine and Rhone. More than half of its electricity comes from hydropower, which uses moving water.

The research shows how changes to snow and ice can affect water far beyond a glacier's edge.
why_it_matters: Swiss water feeds important European rivers, and Switzerland uses hydropower for more than half its electricity. Glacier measurements help explain changes in these water supplies.
